## What this guide will help you understand

Our presentation contains several new terms at once: preprocessing, TF-IDF,
query likelihood, smoothing, BM25, Precision@3, and MAP. It is reasonable to
need the basic ideas before discussing the experiment.

We will build those ideas step by step. Each explanation starts with an
ordinary question, then uses a small example, and finally connects to our code.

**Our main question:** How can a computer decide which document to show first
when someone types a search query?

## How to study

1. Read pages 2-6 to understand the problem and query likelihood.
2. Read pages 7-9 to understand smoothing, TF-IDF, and BM25.
3. Read pages 10-12 to understand evaluation and our actual results.
4. Use page 13 to connect the ideas to Python.
5. Try the questions on page 14 before reading the answers on page 15.
6. Keep page 16 nearby as a glossary and reference list.

Please pause at each **Check your understanding** question. Explain the answer
in your own words before looking at the next page. A calculator is enough for
the worked examples.

**One sentence to keep in mind:** We estimate word probabilities for each
document, then rank documents by how likely their models are to generate the query.

This is a personal study document. The three-document example below is separate
from the 15-document experiment in our presentation.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# 1. What the experiment table means

A search query is the text a user types, such as `search data`. A document is
one item we might retrieve: a web page, an article, or a short text. A collection
is the set of all searchable documents. A ranking is an ordered list of results.

Our experiment table describes four different decisions:

| Row in the slide | Meaning in ordinary language |
|---|---|
| Preprocessing | How we prepare text before counting words |
| Retrieval methods | TF-IDF, Dirichlet query likelihood, and BM25 |
| Language models | Ways to estimate probabilities for query likelihood |
| Evaluation | Precision@3 and MAP show how relevant results are ordered |

## Did we use the query likelihood model?

**Yes.** MLE, JM (0.2), and Dirichlet (20) all feed word probabilities into the
same query-likelihood ranking idea. They differ in how they estimate those
probabilities. TF-IDF and BM25 are separate lexical ranking methods we compare.

| Method label | What it means in our experiment |
|---|---|
| MLE | Query likelihood using observed document word frequencies |
| JM (0.2) | Query likelihood with Jelinek-Mercer smoothing; background weight 0.2 |
| Dirichlet (20) | Query likelihood with Dirichlet smoothing; strength parameter 20 |
| TF-IDF | Weighted word vectors compared using cosine similarity |
| BM25 | A ranking score balancing rarity, repeated terms, and length |

## A useful distinction

A **retrieval method** assigns scores and orders documents. An **evaluation
measure** judges that ordering against relevance labels. Precision@3 and MAP
do not retrieve documents. They help us assess the results.

**Check your understanding:** Which is the ranking method: Dirichlet query
likelihood or Precision@3? Which is the evaluation measure?

{{< pagebreak >}}

# 2. Preprocessing and bag-of-words

A computer needs a consistent way to turn text into countable pieces. A
**token** is one piece of text produced by tokenization. In our experiment,
tokens are lowercase sequences of English letters.

## The exact preprocessing we use

Input: `Search, SEARCH data!`

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| Convert to lowercase | `search, search data!` |
| Extract alphabetic words | `search`, `search`, `data` |
| Count the words | search: 2; data: 1 |

Our tokenizer uses `re.findall(r"[a-z]+", text.lower())`. It removes punctuation
from these tokens and does not keep numbers. It also splits an apostrophe or
hyphen into separate alphabetic runs.

**No stemming** means we do not reduce word forms to a shared root. For example,
`model` and `models` remain different tokens. We also keep stop words such as
`the` and `of`. This tokenizer is an English teaching choice. Khmer text needs
an appropriate word-segmentation strategy.

## Our running collection

We will use these exact three documents on pages 3-9 and 13:

| Document | Text | Token count |
|---|---|---:|
| A | `search search data` | 3 |
| B | `search data data data` | 4 |
| C | `data science` | 2 |

The **vocabulary** contains the distinct words: `search`, `data`, and `science`.
A bag-of-words representation records how often each word appears:

| Document | search | data | science |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 2 | 1 | 0 |
| B | 1 | 3 | 0 |
| C | 0 | 1 | 1 |

The order disappears. `search data search` has the same counts as A.

**Check your understanding:** What is the length of B? Does it have four
vocabulary words, or four tokens?

{{< pagebreak >}}

# 3. Probability and a language model

A probability describes how likely an event is under a model. It ranges from
0 to 1. A value of 0.5 means one half. It does not mean 50 occurrences.

## Imagine drawing a word from a bag

Document A contains three word slips: `search`, `search`, and `data`. If we
randomly select one slip, two of the three slips say `search`.

$$P(\text{search}\mid A)=\frac{2}{3},\qquad
P(\text{data}\mid A)=\frac{1}{3}.$$

Read the vertical bar as **given**: "probability of search, given document A."
We have fixed A as the source from which the word is drawn.

These probabilities add to 1. No slip says `science`, so its probability under
this simple model is 0.

## What makes this a language model?

A language model assigns probabilities to words or sequences of words. Our
small document model describes a probability distribution over the vocabulary.
We build a separate distribution for each document.

| Model | P(search) | P(data) | P(science) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 2/3 | 1/3 | 0 |
| B | 1/4 | 3/4 | 0 |
| C | 0 | 1/2 | 1/2 |

This is a **unigram model**: each word probability is independent of previous
words. A bigram model instead uses one previous word, such as
$P(\text{data}\mid\text{search})$.

In Lecture 2, bigrams retain local word order. Here we choose unigrams to keep
probability estimation simple. A chat model also models language, but our
count-based model only needs word frequencies to score a query.

**Check your understanding:** Why is P(data given B) 3/4 rather than 3/9?
Which source are we drawing from?

{{< pagebreak >}}

# 4. Query likelihood and MLE

Our query is **`search data`**. Query likelihood asks:

> If this document's model randomly produced words, how likely would it be to
> produce the words in our query?

The document does not literally write a query. This is the probability model
we choose to calculate a ranking score.

## Step 1: estimate word probabilities

**MLE** means *maximum likelihood estimation*. In this unigram count model,
it gives the observed proportion of a word inside a document:

$$P_{\mathrm{MLE}}(w\mid d)=\frac{c(w,d)}{|d|}.$$

Here $w$ means a word, $d$ a document, $c(w,d)$ its word count, and $|d|$ the
document's number of tokens. The word "maximum" does not mean choosing only
the document's most frequent word. We estimate a probability for every word.

## Step 2: combine the query words

Under our independence assumption, multiply the probabilities:

$$P(\text{search data}\mid d)
=P(\text{search}\mid d)\,P(\text{data}\mid d).$$

| Document | Calculation | Query likelihood |
|---|---|---:|
| A | (2/3) × (1/3) | 0.2222 |
| B | (1/4) × (3/4) | 0.1875 |
| C | 0 × (1/2) | 0 |

## Step 3: rank from largest to smallest

The ranking is **A, B, C**. A gives the full query a higher probability than B,
even though B contains more instances of `data`.

A high query likelihood is a scoring signal. It is not a guarantee that the
document answers the user's need. Also, 0.2222 is **not** a 22.22% probability
that A is relevant. It is the modeled probability of these query words given A.

**Check your understanding:** For query `data`, would A still rank above B?

{{< pagebreak >}}

# 5. Why we use logs and smoothing

Two separate problems appear when we multiply word probabilities.

## Problem 1: very small products

For a long query, multiplying many probabilities can produce a number too small
for a computer to represent accurately. We therefore add **natural logarithms**:

$$s(d,q)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log P(w_i\mid d).$$

Here the query has $m$ tokens. If a word appears twice, it contributes twice.
The logarithm preserves the ranking because it increases with its input.

| Document | Query likelihood from page 5 | Natural log score |
|---|---:|---:|
| A | 0.222222 | -1.5041 |
| B | 0.187500 | -1.6740 |
| C | 0 | negative infinity |

**Higher is better.** -1.5041 is higher than -1.6740. The ranking is still A, B, C.
A negative log score is normal. It does not mean a negative probability.

## Problem 2: one missing query word

C contains `data`, but it has no `search`. The zero for `search` makes the entire
product zero. A logarithm does not fix this. The log of zero has no finite value,
and the code represents it as negative infinity.

**Smoothing** changes the word probabilities before we calculate the score.
It gives some probability to words missing from a document.

For collection-based smoothing, we first count all three documents together:

| Word | Collection count | Collection probability |
|---|---:|---:|
| search | 3 | 3/9 = 1/3 |
| data | 5 | 5/9 |
| science | 1 | 1/9 |

The collection has **9 tokens**, not 3. Its vocabulary has **3 distinct words**.
We write this background probability as $P(w\mid C_{all})$.

**Check your understanding:** Does taking logs make C's missing-word probability
positive? What step do we need first?

{{< pagebreak >}}

# 6. Jelinek-Mercer smoothing

Jelinek-Mercer, abbreviated **JM**, mixes two distributions: the document's
observed word probabilities and the collection's background probabilities.

$$P_{\mathrm{JM}}(w\mid d)
=(1-\lambda)P_{\mathrm{MLE}}(w\mid d)
+\lambda P(w\mid C_{all}).$$

In our code, $\lambda$ is the **background weight**. With $\lambda=0.2$, we use
80% document probability and 20% background probability. Some sources define
the symbol the other way around, so always check the formula.

## A missing word receives background support

For document C and word `search`:

$$P_{\mathrm{JM}}(\text{search}\mid C)
=0.8(0)+0.2(1/3)=0.0667.$$

For word `data`:

$$P_{\mathrm{JM}}(\text{data}\mid C)
=0.8(1/2)+0.2(5/9)=0.5111.$$

The query likelihood is now approximately $0.0667\times0.5111=0.0341$.
C can receive a usable score even though it misses one query word.

## Results for all three documents

| Document | Smoothed P(search) | Smoothed P(data) | Query likelihood |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 0.6000 | 0.3778 | 0.2267 |
| B | 0.2667 | 0.7111 | 0.1896 |
| C | 0.0667 | 0.5111 | 0.0341 |

The ranking remains A, B, C. **Smoothing can improve probability estimates
without changing the ranking of a particular query.**

If $\lambda$ moves toward 1, the models rely more on the same collection
background and become less different. JM applies the same mixture weight to
every document, regardless of length. The notebook's label **JM (0.2)** refers
to this background weight, not to a measured accuracy of 0.2.

**Check your understanding:** What does $\lambda=0.2$ mean in ordinary words?

{{< pagebreak >}}

# 7. Dirichlet smoothing

Dirichlet smoothing also combines document evidence with the background. It
adds imaginary supporting counts, called **pseudo-counts**.

$$P_{\mu}(w\mid d)=
\frac{c(w,d)+\mu P(w\mid C_{all})}{|d|+\mu}.$$

Read it as: **observed count plus background support, divided by observed length
plus total added support**. The parameter $\mu$ is positive. Fractional
pseudo-counts are allowed.

## A small worked example

Use **$\mu=3$ for this teaching example**. The query is still `search data`.
C has length 2. The background probabilities are 1/3 for `search` and 5/9 for `data`.

$$P_3(\text{search}\mid C)=\frac{0+3(1/3)}{2+3}=\frac15=0.2.$$

$$P_3(\text{data}\mid C)=\frac{1+3(5/9)}{2+3}=\frac{8}{15}=0.5333.$$

So $P(\text{search data}\mid C)=0.2\times0.5333\approx0.1067$.

| Document | Smoothed P(search) | Smoothed P(data) | Query likelihood |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 0.5000 | 0.4444 | 0.2222 |
| B | 0.2857 | 0.6667 | 0.1905 |
| C | 0.2000 | 0.5333 | 0.1067 |

## What does Dirichlet (20) mean in our slide?

Our **actual notebook uses $\mu=20$**, not 3. It is a strength parameter,
not a number of documents or a probability. The background's effective weight is
$\mu/(|d|+\mu)$. With $\mu=20$ and document length 10, it is $20/30=0.667$.
With length 100, it is $20/120=0.167$. Short documents receive more smoothing.

JM fixes the mixture weight directly. Dirichlet lets the weight depend on
length. Neither learns synonyms. Also, the lecture's **add-one** smoothing uses
one pseudo-count per vocabulary word, while Dirichlet uses collection-based support.

**Check your understanding:** At a fixed length, does a larger $\mu$ give more
or less weight to the background?

{{< pagebreak >}}

# 8. Our baseline: TF-IDF cosine similarity

A **baseline** is a comparison method. We compare query likelihood with TF-IDF
to see whether their ranked lists differ on the same queries and documents.

**TF** means term frequency: how often a word appears inside a document.
**IDF** means inverse document frequency: how widely that word occurs across
documents. A word found almost everywhere usually helps distinguish documents
less than a word found in only a few documents.

## The particular version used in our code

Scikit-learn uses smoothed IDF here:

$$\operatorname{idf}(w)=\log\frac{1+N}{1+\operatorname{df}(w)}+1.$$

$N$ is the number of documents. $\operatorname{df}(w)$ counts **documents that
contain the word**, not all occurrences of the word. We multiply raw TF by IDF,
then normalize each vector to length 1.

| Word | Documents containing it | IDF in our three-document example |
|---|---:|---:|
| search | 2 | 1.2877 |
| data | 3 | 1.0000 |
| science | 1 | 1.6931 |

A's weighted vector, ordered as search/data/science, is approximately
$(2.5754,1,0)$. The query `search data` has vector $(1.2877,1,0)$ before normalization.

**Cosine similarity** measures how closely two vectors point in the same
direction. Its formula divides their dot product by their lengths. We already
normalize the vectors, so our code can simply use their dot product.

| Method | What produces the score? | Better score |
|---|---|---|
| TF-IDF cosine | Similarity between weighted vectors | Larger cosine |
| Query likelihood | Probability of query words under a document model | Larger likelihood or log likelihood |

Both methods use word counts. Their numerical scores have different meanings.
Compare their rankings and relevance metrics, rather than comparing a cosine
of 0.7 directly with a log score of -5.

**Check your understanding:** `search` occurs twice in A. Does that count twice
toward its document frequency?

{{< pagebreak >}}

# 9. BM25: a balanced word-matching score

BM25 ranks documents using query words. It keeps three useful ideas:

1. **Rare words matter more.** A query word in fewer documents gets a higher IDF.
2. **Repeating a word helps, but the benefit levels off.** This is term-frequency saturation.
3. **Length is compared with the collection average.** A document is not penalized just for being longer than a short one.

A common BM25 formula is:

$$\operatorname{BM25}(d,q)=\sum_{t\in q}\operatorname{IDF}(t)
\frac{f(t,d)(k_1+1)}{f(t,d)+k_1(1-b+b|d|/\operatorname{avgdl})}.$$

Here $f(t,d)$ is the count of word $t$ in document $d$, $|d|$ is the document's
length, and $\operatorname{avgdl}$ is the average document length. BM25 outputs
a **ranking score**, not a probability that the document generated the query.

## What do k1 and b control?

- **$k_1$** controls how quickly repeated word counts level off. Common starting
  value: 1.2.
- **$b$** controls how strongly document length affects the score. At 0, length
  is ignored. At 1, length is fully normalized. Common starting value: 0.75.

These values work as starting settings; a search system may tune them on
separate development queries.

## Lecture 5's pizza example

The query is `pizza oven`. The judged relevant documents are D1 and D3. D2
repeats `pizza` many times but does not answer the user's need. D3 is a long,
relevant guide.

| Method | First two results | Precision@2 |
|---|---|---:|
| TF-IDF cosine | D1, D2 | 0.5 |
| BM25 | D1, D3 | 1.0 |

BM25 limits D2's repetition advantage and keeps the long relevant document D3
near the top. This is Lecture 5's separate six-document example, not our
15-document project experiment.

**Check your understanding:** If a term appears 20 times instead of 10 in a
document, does BM25's term contribution necessarily double?

{{< pagebreak >}}

# 10. Two measures for a ranked list

First, a person needs to mark which documents are relevant to the query. A
relevant document helps meet the user's information need; matching a word by
itself is not enough.

Suppose a ranking starts this way:

| Rank | Result | Relevant? |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | D1 | Yes |
| 2 | D2 | No |
| 3 | D3 | Yes |

## Precision@3: are the first three results useful?

$$P@3=\frac{\text{relevant results among the first 3}}{3}
=\frac{2}{3}\approx0.667.$$

Two of the three results shown are relevant.

## Average Precision and MAP: are relevant results near the top?

**Average Precision (AP)** checks how many relevant results have appeared at
each relevant position, then averages those precision values. In our small
example, relevant documents are at ranks 1 and 3:

$$AP=\frac{1/1+2/3}{2}=0.833.$$

**Mean Average Precision (MAP)** is the average AP across all queries. P@3
focuses on the top three; MAP uses the positions of relevant documents across
the full ranking. Together they give us a clear view of early usefulness and
overall ordering.

**Check your understanding:** Does MAP = 1 mean all documents are relevant?

{{< pagebreak >}}

# 11. Reading our actual notebook results

Our project has **15 teaching documents and 5 queries**. The following are
mean scores across those queries. This is not the same collection as the
three-document examples in this guide or the pizza example from Lecture 5.

| Method | Precision@3 | MAP |
|---|---:|---:|
| TF-IDF cosine | 0.600 | 0.900 |
| Dirichlet query likelihood | 0.600 | 1.000 |
| BM25 | 0.600 | 0.900 |

All three methods find the same average number of relevant documents in their
top three. Dirichlet places the relevant documents earlier across the full
rankings on these five queries.

## Why does Q5 change the MAP result?

For query `car coverage`, the intended relevant document D13 discusses vehicle
insurance. D14 discusses parking and repeats the exact word `car`.

- TF-IDF and BM25 put D14 first and D13 second. Since there is one relevant
document, AP = 1/2 = 0.5 for that query.
- Dirichlet puts D13 first, so AP = 1.0.
- On the other four queries, all three methods have AP = 1.0.

So MAP is 0.9 for TF-IDF and BM25, and 1.0 for Dirichlet. P@3 remains 0.6
because the first three positions contain the same number of relevant results.

## What these results do not establish

This is a tiny collection with five queries and our own relevance labels. These
scores explain the behavior of this example; they do not establish that
Dirichlet is generally better. We would need more independently judged queries
and evaluation on data held apart from any parameter tuning.

**Check your understanding:** Could two methods have the same P@3 but different
MAP? Why?

# 12. Connecting the ideas to Python

The project shares one implementation between the notebook and the Streamlit
app. This small example runs all three comparison methods on the insurance
query:

```python
experiment = RetrievalExperiment(documents)
query = "car coverage"

for method in ["tfidf", "dirichlet", "bm25"]:
    ranking, unknown = experiment.rank(
        query,
        method=method,
        mu=20,
        k1=1.2,
        b=0.75,
    )
    print(method, ranking[:3], "unknown words:", unknown)
```

Each method returns a list of document IDs and scores. The scores have
method-specific meanings, so compare the **order** of the documents, not the
raw scores across methods. For our Q5 example, TF-IDF and BM25 put D14 first;
Dirichlet puts D13 first.

**Try it:** Change the query to `language model`. Which documents rise to the
top? Then select BM25 in the Streamlit app and change $k_1$ or $b$.

# 14. Answers with reasons

1. **Tokens:** `data`, `data`, `science`. Counts are data: 2 and science: 1.
   Lowercasing lets `DATA` and `data` match.

2. **Length = 4.** P(search given B) = 1/4. P(data given B) = 3/4. We divide
   by B's token count because B is the model's source.

3. **(3/4) × (3/4) = 9/16 = 0.5625.** Each query token contributes a factor.
   Repeated query words are not removed from the likelihood calculation.

4. **C has no `search`, so one factor is zero.** The whole product becomes
   zero. Logs produce negative infinity for that case. We need smoothing
   before calculating logs.

5. **P(search given collection) = 3/9 = 1/3.** JM gives C
   $0.8(0)+0.2(1/3)=1/15\approx0.0667$.

6. **(0 + 3 × 1/3)/(2 + 3) = 1/5 = 0.2.** The parameter 3 is total
   background pseudo-count strength. It is not the number of documents, even
   though our teaching collection happens to have three documents.

7. **The benefit levels off.** $k_1$ controls how quickly the term-frequency
   benefit saturates; $b$ controls how much document length affects the score.

8. **P@3 = 2/3. AP = (1 + 2/3)/2 = 0.833.** The relevant results appear at
   ranks one and three, so we average precision at those positions.

9. **AP = (1/2 + 2/4)/2 = 0.5.** MAP is the mean of the two AP values:
   $(0.5+2/3)/2=7/12\approx0.583$.

10. **The relevant documents were ordered before irrelevant documents for
    these five queries.** This is a small result under our labels. We need
    more independent relevance judgments and testing on separate queries.

11. **No.** A word absent from the whole collection has background probability
    zero. Our app reports and drops unknown words, and returns no ranking when
    every query word is unknown. This is an explicit policy.

12. **Possible explanation:** We lowercase and tokenize the text, then compare
    TF-IDF cosine, Dirichlet query likelihood, and BM25. Precision@3 measures
    relevance in the first three results; MAP measures how early relevant
    documents appear across the full ranking.

**Practice sentence:** Query likelihood estimates the chance of the query
words under each document model. Dirichlet smoothing supports words missing from
a document. TF-IDF compares weighted vectors. BM25 balances rarity, repetition,
and document length. We evaluate the resulting order with Precision@3 and MAP.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# 15. Glossary and further reading

| Term | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| Token | One piece of text after tokenization |
| Vocabulary | The set of distinct tokens |
| Bag-of-words | Word counts with word order ignored |
| Language model | A model that assigns probabilities to text |
| Unigram | A single word; here, modeled without previous-word context |
| Likelihood | How probable the observed query is under a fixed model |
| MLE | Probability estimation from observed relative frequencies here |
| Smoothing | Adjusting estimates to support unseen document terms |
| Background | Word probabilities estimated from the whole collection |
| Baseline | A comparison method |
| BM25 | A ranking score that balances rare words, repeated terms, and document length |
| $k_1$ | BM25 setting that controls how quickly term frequency levels off |
| $b$ | BM25 setting that controls the document-length adjustment |
| Precision@3 | The share of the first three results that are relevant |
| AP | Average precision at the positions of relevant documents |
| MAP | Mean AP across queries |
| Relevant | Useful for the query's intended information need |
| Parameter | A setting such as JM's 0.2 or Dirichlet's 20 |
| OOV | Out of vocabulary: a term absent from the collection |

## A few points to remember

**Probability of the query and probability of relevance are different.** Equal
document priors let us rank by query likelihood through Bayes' rule, but the
score remains a modeling assumption. **Lower perplexity measures better text
prediction**, which does not automatically mean better retrieval. **Smoothing
supports missing words, but does not understand synonyms or restore word order.**

- **Evaluation:** Manning et al., [Evaluation of ranked retrieval results](https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/html/htmledition/evaluation-of-ranked-retrieval-results-1.html).
- **Implementation:** [Scikit-learn TfidfVectorizer](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfVectorizer.html).

All small numerical examples are worked teaching examples. The page-12 results
come from this project's executed notebook and CSV files. The guide's editable
source is `learning/learning-guide.qmd`. Render it from the repository root with
`quarto render learning/learning-guide.qmd`.
